title: Ramana Maharshi (Who Am I?)
hook: a restless elephant, a chain, and the helps Ramana allows

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ramana Maharshi's stick at the fire: when a thought comes, ask to whom it came, then who am I? Did one circling thought loosen when you asked? Your line was to whom did this come? Day nine hundred fifty-one.

An elephant walking down a street swings its trunk from side to side. It grabs at a banana stall, a branch, the edge of someone's cart. Nothing malicious. A trunk just reaches. Now give that elephant a chain to hold in its trunk. It carries the chain, and the reaching stops. Ramana Maharshi uses that picture in Who Am I?, in the middle of a plain, practical answer about how to steady a mind that won't settle.
screen: `A TRUNK THAT GRABS AT EVERYTHING.` → `GIVE IT A CHAIN TO HOLD.` → `RAMANA WAS PRACTICAL.`

segments.voice: The question who am I? is the main road in the text. But Ramana is asked about other practices, and he doesn't wave them away. He gives each one a place. First, the breath. The mind and the breath, he says, come from the same source. So when the breath is controlled, the mind quiets too. But he adds a warning: that quiet lasts only as long as the breath is held still. When the breath moves again, the mind gets up and goes back to its old wandering. Breath control is a help, he says, not the destination. Then, repeating a name of God, or resting the attention on a form of God. Here's where the elephant comes in. The mind, like that trunk, keeps reaching for one thing after another. Give it one thing to hold, a name, a form, and it steadies. A mind that's held steady on one thing, Ramana says, finds the inquiry easier. So those practices aren't rivals to the question. They're ways to quiet the trunk so the question can be asked. Notice the tone. He isn't telling anyone their practice is wrong. A person who chants, a person who watches the breath, a person who asks who am I, each gets a place, with a plain note about what each one does and how long its help lasts. Tomorrow, the last of these four days: where Ramana says happiness actually lives.
screen: `THE MAIN ROAD: WHO AM I?` · `BREATH AND MIND SHARE ONE SOURCE.` · `A NAME OF GOD STEADIES THE MIND.` · then, large: `GIVE THE TRUNK A CHAIN.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably. For the first part of the sit, give the trunk a chain. Choose one thing to hold: the breath going in and out at the nose, or, if you pray, a name of God that belongs to your own practice, repeated quietly. Each time the attention reaches for something else, bring it back to the one thing. Then, when the mind feels a little steadier, let the chain go and ask once, softly: who am I? Rest wherever that question leaves you. The bell holds the time.
Ramana Maharshi. The teacher of who am I?, who also made room for the breath and the name of God as ways to steady a reaching mind.
Your line: give the trunk a chain. Today, when your attention starts grabbing at everything, give it one chain: three slow breaths, or a name you love. Day nine hundred fifty-one.

howItsDone: Some who follow Ramana combine self-inquiry with chanting a divine name, meditating on a form of God, or watching the breath, using these to steady the mind before or alongside asking 'who am I?'.

fork.setup: an elephant's trunk keeps grabbing at stalls and carts as it walks. what steadies it, in Ramana's picture?
options: tie the trunk down so it can't move.
give it a chain to hold.
lead it down an empty street.
fork.reveal: given one thing to hold, the trunk stops reaching. a name or form of God does the same for the mind, Ramana says, and a steady mind finds the inquiry easier.

original.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: prana, the breath and life-force. Ramana says breath and mind share one source.

trapdoor: what you thought: Ramana only taught one technique, and nothing else counts.
what it means: who am I? is the main road, but breath control and the name of God get a place as helps.
what a scholar hears: a place for each practice, with a plain note on what it does: breath quiets the mind only for a while; one-pointed attention prepares it for inquiry.
recall: watching until the dust is gone

notes: All paraphrase. Confirm in Nan Yar: mind and breath share a source; breath control gives only temporary quiet; japa or meditation on forms of God makes the mind one-pointed; and the elephant-trunk-and-chain image (the hook's banana stall and cart are illustrative embellishments of that image).
The closing remark on generosity is interpretive; soften or cut if a Keeper prefers.

Editor pass: cut the narrator's praise ('that generosity is worth noticing', 'something about him that's easy to miss') and the stock 'seat at the table'; the closing now restates what the text says each practice does.
